title: New Grub Street: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to New Grub Street Unpacked — a close reading of George Gissing's great novel of literary ambition, poverty, and the marketplace of words.
New Grub Street was published in 1891, and it remains one of the most unsettling and honest books ever written about what it costs to make art for a living.

Over the course of this episode, we'll be moving through the novel passage by passage — its characters, its arguments, its extraordinary atmosphere — with three guests who bring very different eyes to Gissing's world.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels than perhaps any living reader — he hears prose the way a conductor hears a score, and he brings that performer's ear to everything we discuss today.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and a critic of the old school — in the very best sense — who believes the novel is above all a moral form, a test of individual character.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of power — who pays and who suffers, and why the system is arranged to keep it that way.
Welcome to all three of you.
Now — the title itself is a provocation.
Grub Street: that old London byword for hack writing, poverty, and literary failure.
Gissing plants his flag in that tradition and dares us to take it seriously.
Oliver — as someone who has spent his life inside the rhythms of great prose, what is your first sense of what Gissing is doing with this world he's built?
The first thing you notice — reading aloud or reading to yourself — is that Gissing's London is almost physically present on the page.
He doesn't describe poverty the way a social reformer would, with statistics and horror.
He describes it the way a great novelist does — with texture, with detail, with a kind of terrible specificity.
There's a passage Daniel is going to talk about in a moment — a penny reading-room at the top of a building — that is one of the most evocative settings in Victorian fiction.
Gissing takes you up those stairs, floor by floor, and by the time you reach the writing room at the top, you feel the whole weight of literary aspiration trapped under a sloping blue ceiling.
That's what great novelists do — they make the physical world carry the emotional argument.
I think Oliver is quite right about the texture — and I'd add that Gissing's great subject is not poverty as such, but the predicament of the educated man confronting poverty.
That is a far more particular and interesting subject, and one that requires a novelist of considerable psychological insight.
Johnson knew something of this.
The original Grub Street was populated not by the ignorant but by the overqualified — men of talent who found no market for what they could actually do.
Gissing inherits that tradition and gives it a Victorian form — the three-volume novel, the circulating library, the magazine market.
What interests me most is whether his characters have the moral resources to meet that challenge — and in many cases, I'm afraid, they do not.
I want to pick up on that reading-room passage, because I think it repays very close attention.
Gissing takes us up through this building floor by floor — newspapers, magazines, chess, refreshments — and each floor is a rung on a social ladder that goes nowhere.
And then you arrive at the writing room, and listen to how he describes it:

"The walls of this last retreat were of blue plaster and sloped inwards from the floor; along them stood school desks with benches, and in one place was suspended a ragged and dirty card announcing that paper and envelopes could be purchased downstairs."
A retreat — he calls it a retreat, which is already rich — but the walls slope inward.
This is a room that is literally contracting around the people who aspire to write in it.
The decorations are ink blotches and scribbling — the residue of all the failed work that has passed through before.

Edmund says the question is whether Gissing's characters have the moral resources to meet their situation — but I'd say Gissing is asking a prior question: whether the situation permits moral resources to operate at all.
That is an interesting formulation, Daniel, but I think it risks absolving the characters of agency — which is precisely what Gissing does not do.
He shows us characters who make choices — bad ones, frequently — and the consequences of those choices.
The system, as you call it, provides the conditions — but the characters provide the responses.
For me the comedy and the tragedy are inseparable in this novel, and that becomes wonderfully clear when Reardon starts talking about the successful writers — the ones who've made it.
There's a marvellous passage where Reardon holds forth on these comfortable, well-connected men — and the mixture of contempt and envy and wounded pride is pitch-perfect.
He says — and this is Reardon speaking, remember, a man eating a very squalid feast indeed —
"They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school men, University men, club men, society men."
The rhythm of that list — public-school men, University men, club men, society men — is magnificent.
Each category is one more door closed to Reardon, and Gissing makes you feel the closing of each one.
And then — the magnificent twist — he says it would be small-minded to feel rancour, but, by Apollo, he knows they'd change places if the work were justly weighed.
And that phrase — if the work were justly weighed — is the crux of the novel's argument, isn't it.
The literary market does not weigh justly.
It weighs by access — by who went to which school, who belongs to which club, who knows which editor.
Reardon calls it small-minded to feel rancour — but the novel as a whole refuses that pious restraint.
Gissing is angry on behalf of his characters even when they cannot afford to be angry themselves.
And that anger, as Daniel says, is given its most complete and devastating expression in Edwin Reardon — the novel's central figure, its great study in unravelling.
We'll turn next to Reardon himself — his ambitions, his paralysis, and the slow-motion collapse of a man who could not make the compromise the market demanded.
We've been mapping the machinery of Grub Street — the market, the pressures, the brutal arithmetic of literary survival.
Now I want to turn to the man who is most visibly crushed by that machine: Edwin Reardon.
Reardon is one of those characters who makes you want to grab the author by the lapels and say: why are you doing this to him?
And then you realise Gissing is doing it because it's true — pitilessly, exactly true.
The physical description alone, in chapter fifteen, stops you cold.
"at thirty-three he would generally have been taken for forty."
Six words, and you feel the whole weight of those twelve months pressing down on him.
Gissing doesn't editorialise — he just gives you the stooped walk, the hesitation in speech, the eyes with that wandering, sometimes wild expression.
A performer reading that aloud has almost nothing to do — the prose has already done it.
What strikes me is how carefully Gissing distinguishes between defeat inflicted from without and defeat accepted from within.
Reardon is not simply a victim of a cruel market — he is a man whose character has a particular fragility.
There is a passage from chapter four that I keep returning to, where Reardon articulates his own artistic conscience.
"There's the shrinking from conscious insincerity of workmanship — which most of the writers nowadays seem never to feel."
That is a man with a genuine moral imagination about his craft.
And that very conscience — that refusal to say 'it's good enough for the market' — is precisely what the market punishes him for.
Tragedy, in the classical sense, requires a man of stature brought low by a flaw inseparable from his virtue.
I don't want to quarrel with the word 'tragedy,' but I think we need to be careful about where we locate the fault.
Because Reardon himself locates it with remarkable precision — and it isn't in his character.
In chapter fifteen, he says it directly, and I want to read the full charge because it's extraordinary.
"The world has no pity on a man who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money.
You may be a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn't take pity on you you will starve by the roadside.
Society is as blind and brutal as fate."
That is not a man sinking into self-pity — that is an indictment.
And notice he does something almost ruthlessly honest: he acknowledges his own partial responsibility, then insists the system's cruelty is real regardless.
I don't dispute the indictment, but I notice Gissing also shows us exactly how Reardon's own history has unmade him.
In chapter six, Reardon traces the internal biography of his failure with extraordinary self-awareness.
"A temperament like mine can't pass through such a violent change of conditions without being greatly affected;
I have never since been the man I was before I left England."
The happiness of his marriage — the very thing that was supposed to sustain him — is what broke the equilibrium he had so slowly built.
There is something almost Johnsonian in that: the recognition that a man is shaped, and can be reshaped, by his particular circumstances — and not always upward.
And that collapse gets mirrored — with devastating efficiency — in the marriage itself.
Chapter twelve has a sentence that I think is one of the finest in the book for sheer compressed grief.
"Their relations to each other — not long ago an inexhaustible topic — would not bear spoken comment;
both were too conscious of the danger-signal when they looked that way."
The danger-signal — that's the phrase that gets me every time.
Not a quarrel, not an explosion — just this shared, silent agreement not to look at what the marriage has become.
Gissing is writing about the most intimate form of loneliness: two people in the same room, both choosing not to see.
And notice what Amy has done in the meantime: she's been talking to her mother, possibly to others — the marriage is already being evaluated by outside opinion.
Class respectability is doing its work even inside the home.
And then in chapter seventeen, Reardon has this horrible moment of perception about Amy's voice.
"With just such accent he had heard a wrangling woman retort upon her husband at the street corner.
Is there then no essential difference between a woman of this world and one of that?"
Now, Reardon means that as a question about human nature — but what it actually reveals is how poverty has stripped away the class performance both of them depended on.
The 'essential difference' he's mourning was never essential — it was always purchased.
That is a sharp reading, though I'd resist collapsing Amy entirely into a class mechanism.
Reardon's accusation in chapter sixteen is worth holding up to the light as well.
"It seems to me, Amy, that your one desire is to get away from me, on whatever terms."
What's devastating is the phrase 'on whatever terms' — it implies she no longer cares about the terms, that the marriage has lost even its power to wound her.
Whether that is fair to Amy is another matter — Gissing is generous enough to leave that ambiguous.
But Reardon's tragedy is in some ways the tragedy of a man who can articulate his own ruin with complete lucidity and change nothing.
Lucidity without agency — that's the thing that makes him genuinely tragic rather than merely pathetic.
He sees every stage of the descent with terrible clarity.
He knows exactly what 'good enough for the market' means, and exactly what it would cost him to do it.
And he does it anyway — and it destroys him anyway.
Reardon sees the trap with perfect clarity — and steps into it regardless.
Which makes it all the more striking to set him beside someone who sees the same trap and is determined, absolutely determined, not to be caught in it.
After the break, we turn to Jasper Milvain — the man who has decided that if the market is the game, he will play it without apology.
We've been watching Reardon collapse under the weight of his own artistic conscience — unable to bend, unable to sell.
Now I want to turn to the man who is, in almost every respect, Reardon's photographic negative: Jasper Milvain.
Jasper Milvain is one of the great comic-serious creations in Victorian fiction — and I say that with complete conviction.
He is utterly shameless, but Gissing never quite lets you hate him, because he is so refreshingly honest about his own shamelessness.
Right at the start, he sits down with his sisters and delivers what I can only call his manifesto — with tremendous brio.
"Literature nowadays is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman."
The rhythm of that is extraordinary — the little parenthesis about men of genius, airily dismissed, and then the verdict landing like a hammer.
Gissing gives Jasper all the best tunes, and he knows it.
I think one must be careful not to mistake fluency for wisdom — which is precisely the mistake Jasper himself makes about Jasper.
What strikes me in that opening declaration is how completely Milvain identifies his own convenience with historical necessity.
He tells his sisters, in that same passage, that Reardon "sells a manuscript as if he lived in Sam Johnson's Grub Street" — as though the comparison settles the matter entirely.
But Johnson's Grub Street produced the Dictionary, the Rambler, the Lives of the Poets.
Jasper's Grub Street — supplied, as he puts it, with telegraphic communication — produces reviews of pompous idiots who give good dinners.
The market, in this novel, is not a liberating force.
It is a machine that rewards the most cynical possible relationship to one's own talent.
Edmund is exactly right that the market rewards cynicism — but I think we need to press harder on why that matters structurally.
Jasper doesn't simply choose cynicism as a personal failing.
He announces it, quite calmly, as a discovered truth about the conditions of literary production in 1882.
And Gissing — crucially — allows Amy Reardon to say almost exactly the same thing.
Her line to her husband is as cold and clear as anything Jasper utters — listen to this:
"Art must be practised as a trade, at all events in our time. This is the age of trade."
She goes on: "Of course if one refuses to be of one's time, and yet hasn't the means to live independently, what can result but breakdown and wretchedness?"
Now — Amy is not a villain.
She is a reasonably intelligent woman who has absorbed exactly the lesson the literary market teaches anyone who pays attention.
The horror Gissing is documenting is not individual corruption — it is ideological saturation.
Daniel's phrase — ideological saturation — is exactly right, but what I find so startling is how gleefully Jasper inhabits it.
There is a passage where he essentially confesses everything — his laziness, his contempt for his readers, his absolute indifference to literary value — and presents it as a programme for success.
"Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value; I shall always despise the people I write for. But my path will be that of success."
The punctuation of that — the full stop after 'write for,' the 'But' — it's a man shrugging at his own soul.
And Gissing writes it without a single word of authorial condemnation.
He just... lets Jasper stand there, perfectly illuminated by his own confession.
I want to linger on the word 'despise' — because I think it is the key to Milvain's character, and not in the way Daniel's reading would suggest.
Jasper's contempt for his audience is not a class grievance — it is a moral vacancy.
He lacks what Johnson would have called — what any serious critic must call — a sense of literary obligation.
And Gissing is, I think, quite precise about the practical shape of that vacancy.
Consider the passage where Jasper describes writing laudatory reviews of a man called Billington — 'pompous idiocy, of course, but he lives in a big house and gives dinners.'
"It's the easiest thing in the world to write laudation; only an inexperienced grumbler would declare it was easier to find fault."
The wit is perfectly turned — and perfectly hollow.
Corruption dressed in the clothes of efficiency.
I don't disagree with Edmund about the moral vacancy — but I think Gissing wants us to see that the system actively selects for it.
Jasper says it explicitly, with an honesty that ought to make us uncomfortable rather than merely contemptuous.
He is speaking about his refusal to let anything interfere with his advancement — and he frames it like a business plan:
"I shall never write for writing's sake, only to make money. All my plans and efforts will have money in view — all. I shan't allow anything to come in the way of my material advancement."
That final word — 'all' — repeated like a vow.
Gissing is showing us a man who has fully internalised the logic of capital and mistaken it for self-knowledge.
And the tragedy — if we can call it that — is that he is probably right about the outcome.
What I keep returning to is Gissing's refusal to make Jasper unlikeable in the conventional sense.
He is energetic, articulate, amusing company — and Gissing gives him the novel's most vivid set-pieces.

That passage where he lays out his vision of the new Grub Street — 'supplied with telegraphic communication, it knows what literary fare is in demand in every part of the world' — it crackles with genuine excitement.
And the reader feels that excitement too, which is the point.
Gissing is not writing a morality play where the bad man wears a sign.
He is writing a novel in which the seductive and the corrupt are, disturbingly, the same thing.
Milvain's gambit, then: a man who sees the literary market with perfect clarity and chooses, with open eyes, to be its most willing instrument.
Which raises the question of who else in this novel has no choice but to serve that same machine — and without anything like Jasper's breezy confidence.
After the break, we turn to Marian Yule — buried in the Reading Room of the British Museum, copying other men's ideas for a father who barely sees her.

segments.title: Marian's Bind: Labour and Longing in the Library

utterances.text: We've been tracing Jasper Milvain's calculating ascent through the literary marketplace — his eye always on the prize, his conscience always negotiable.
Now I want to turn to someone who inhabits that same world with none of Milvain's armour — Marian Yule, whose story Gissing tells with devastating tenderness.
Marian is, for me, one of the great quiet catastrophes in Victorian fiction.
She barely raises her voice in the entire novel, and yet Gissing contrives to make her suffering absolutely deafening.
There's that passage in Chapter Eight where she goes to her room and weeps — and Gissing renders the whole of her existence in a single sentence.
"She was not a woman, but a mere machine for reading and writing."
Six words of verdict after the dash — and Gissing just lets them sit there.
He doesn't fuss over it, he doesn't explain it — that's the mark of a writer absolutely in command of his material.
That phrase is doing something very precise, and I think Oliver is right to let it breathe.
The word is "machine" — not slave, not servant, machine.
Gissing is describing the reduction of a human being to a unit of literary production — exactly the logic of industrial capital applied to intellectual labour.
And notice the question Gissing immediately follows it with: "Did her father never think of this?"
Alfred Yule extracts his daughter's labour just as surely as the publishers extract his.
The exploitation runs through the family structure itself — there's no sanctuary from the market, not even at home.
One can grant the economic observation without quite accepting the framework, I think.
What strikes me about Marian is not chiefly her position in any system of exchange, but the quality of her perception — the moral and intellectual acuity she brings to her situation.
Gissing is at pains to tell us exactly how she sees the world.
"Her candour was allied with clear insight into the possibilities of falsehood; she was not readily the victim of illusion."
That is not the portrait of a victim — that is the portrait of someone who sees clearly, and suffers all the more for seeing clearly.
Gissing understood — as the great moralists always do — that lucidity is a form of burden, not merely a gift.
Edmund's put his finger on something I keep returning to when I read these passages aloud.
There's an extraordinary scene in the Museum — the Reading Room — where Marian simply stops pretending to work.
The fog outside, the headachy air inside, the books open and useless before her — Gissing builds the atmosphere with a kind of grim relish.
And then she arrives at a question that I think is the moral centre of the entire novel.
"What unspeakable folly! To write — was not that the joy and the privilege of one who had an urgent message for the world?"
"Unspeakable folly" — that exclamation point is doing tremendous work for Gissing.
It's Marian's rage breaking the surface for just a moment before she pushes it back down.
That passage in the Museum is where I think Gissing comes closest to an explicit critique — and then pulls back from it.
Marian sees it: the world already has more good literature than anyone can read in a lifetime.
And yet she is here, as Gissing puts it, "exhausting herself in the manufacture of printed stuff which no one even pretended to be more than a commodity for the day's market."
Commodity — Gissing uses that word deliberately, I'm certain of it.
Literature has been stripped of any claim to truth or beauty — it is simply a thing to be produced, sold, and forgotten.
Marian knows this, and it hollows her out.
I would resist the idea that Gissing intends this as purely structural indictment.
Because Gissing also shows us Marian capable of something the marketplace cannot account for — hope.
The concluding movement of these reflections is one of the most luminous passages in the book.
"She could labour on in the valley of the shadow of books, for a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment strike into its musty gloom."
The valley of the shadow of books — it is an audacious borrowing from the Twenty-Third Psalm, and Gissing earns every syllable of it.
Marian has not been defeated by the system Daniel describes — she has found, within herself, the capacity to endure it.
That is a moral achievement, not merely a psychological one.
The Psalms reference is exactly right, and I think it captures something about Gissing's register here that we shouldn't rush past.
He is writing in a tradition of suffering that is ancient and serious — and then he appends "musty gloom," which is pure Gissing: the bathos is the point.
The sacred and the sordid pressed right up against each other — the Reading Room as vale of tears, smelling of old bindings and fog.
And yet the sunshine is real to Marian — and we believe her, because Gissing has made us believe her.
What's striking is that even Marian's hope is shadowed — the sunshine is only a possibility, only a ray, and the gloom of those stacks remains.
Gissing seems to hold sentiment and its undoing in the same sentence — and that tonal balancing act, the grief that tips into the wryly absurd, brings us naturally to what we want to explore next.
Because Gissing is also — against all odds — extremely funny, and that dark comic gift is something we haven't yet given its proper due.

segments.title: Wit and Gloom: Gissing's Comic Register

utterances.text: We've been sitting with Marian's exhaustion — the grinding, joyless labour of the British Museum Reading Room.
But Gissing is not only a novelist of despair — he is, at moments, a wickedly funny one.
Oliver, you've spent more time inside this novel's prose than almost anyone — where does the comedy live?
It lives in Jasper Milvain, almost entirely.
He is the character Gissing could not quite bring himself to condemn, because Jasper is too entertaining to condemn.
He opens the novel telling his sisters — and us — exactly what kind of book we are inside.
He says, with complete seriousness:

"Writing is a business. Get together half-a-dozen fair specimens of the Sunday-school prize; study them; discover the essential points of such composition; hit upon new attractions; then go to work methodically, so many pages a day."
He is absolutely earnest — and that is what makes it devastating.
The joke, if it is a joke, is that Jasper has thought it all through and the logic is impeccable.
There is a strong case, I think, for reading Jasper as a Restoration wit transplanted into a Victorian novel.
He says things one is not supposed to say, and says them beautifully.
What Gissing has done — and this is rather subtle — is give the cynic all the best speeches.
Jasper declares, for instance, that he would willingly write novels "out-trashing the trashiest that ever sold fifty thousand copies" — if only he had the skill.
And then he delivers the proposition one cannot easily refute:
"To please the vulgar you must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity."
One may disapprove, but one cannot fault the formulation.
The wit is real — I won't argue with either of you there.
But what Gissing is describing through Jasper is not merely a personality — it is a structural condition.
The market has separated the question of value from the question of quality.
Jasper understands this completely and simply proceeds accordingly.
The comedy is the comedy of perfect adaptation — the organism that has evolved precisely to fit its poisoned environment.
Daniel's right, but I want to push back just slightly on the word 'adaptation.'
Because there are figures in this novel who do not adapt, and Gissing watches them with a different kind of comedy — blacker, colder.
Think of Fadge — the editor of The Current, and his philosophy of literary attack.
Gissing gives us this absolutely magnificent formulation:
"To assail an author without increasing the number of his readers is the perfection of journalistic skill."
You could put that line in a guide to media ethics today and nobody would blink.
The malice is so perfectly calibrated it becomes an art form in itself.
What strikes me about that line is the way Gissing holds two thoughts in perfect tension.
He is condemning Fadge, yes — flippancy is described as "the most hopeless form of intellectual vice."
And yet Gissing cannot suppress his admiration for the sheer professionalism of it.
This is a novelist who despises the market and understands it with frightening intimacy.
That intimacy is earned, of course — Gissing lived it.
But the darkest comedy in the novel, for me, is Sykes.
Not Jasper with his brilliant cynicism, not Fadge with his poisoned pin-points — but this minor figure glimpsed at a public writing desk.
Gissing describes him: shabby tweeds, moulting silk hat, the face of a habitual drinker — and yet fully seized by inspiration.
"The veins of his forehead were dilated, and his chin pushed forward in a way that made one think of a racing horse."
The system has reduced this man to writing in a public room in borrowed clothes, and the image Gissing reaches for is nobility — a racing horse in full stride.
That is the novel's deepest comedy — or its deepest grief.
The description of Sykes is extraordinary to read aloud.
There is this long, almost breathless sentence before the racing horse image — the coat-sleeve turned back, the flannel shirt of "singular colour," the collar unbuttoned.

"With coat-sleeve turned back, so as to give free play to his right hand and wrist, revealing meanwhile a flannel shirt of singular colour, and with his collar unbuttoned — to leave his throat at ease as he bent myopically over the paper, he was writing at express speed."
Gissing gives us every shabby detail and then — the ardour of composition.
The comedy and the dignity arrive in the same breath.
Comedy and dignity in the same breath — that is a rather good description of what Gissing does with prose style itself.
How does the form of the novel — the way it is actually built, sentence by sentence — serve and sometimes strain under the weight of all this material?
That is where we go next.

segments.title: Form and Decay: How Gissing Tells New Grub Street

utterances.text: We've been talking about the comedy in Gissing — the dark wit that makes New Grub Street bearable.
But that wit exists inside a very particular formal ambition — a way of telling this story that is itself a kind of argument.
Edmund, you've been sitting with the passages where Gissing lays bare his own aesthetic — and it starts, remarkably, with a character.
It does — and the character is Harold Biffen, who is in some ways the most philosophically serious figure in the novel.
Biffen is writing a novel called Mr Bailey, Grocer — which tells you everything.
And in a late-night conversation with Reardon, he articulates a theory of fiction that is quite breathtaking in its rigour.
He calls it — and the phrase is magnificent — the sphere of the ignobly decent.
He says: 'I want to deal with the essentially unheroic, with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the mercy of paltry circumstance.'
'The mercy of paltry circumstance' — one could spend an hour on that phrase alone.
It captures something Gissing understood viscerally: that most human suffering is not tragic — it is merely grinding.
What I love about that passage is that Biffen takes aim at both Zola and Dickens in the same breath — which requires considerable nerve.
He says Zola's vilest figures become heroic from the place they fill in a strongly imagined drama.
And then Dickens — well, Dickens would have made that overheard lovers' scene ludicrous, which Biffen calls 'a gross injustice.'
What Biffen wants instead is — and this is the killer line — something unutterably tedious.
He writes: 'The result will be something unutterably tedious. Precisely. That is the stamp of the ignobly decent life.'
A novelist who sets out to write something unutterably tedious — and means it as a manifesto.
There is something gloriously paradoxical about Gissing finding the most electrifying character in the book to be the one arguing for total dullness.
I want to press on what Biffen is actually doing politically — because his theory is not just aesthetic, it is a provocation about whose life counts as material for art.
The vast majority who are at the mercy of paltry circumstance — that phrase is doing class work.
Biffen is saying: the literary tradition has systematically excluded ordinary working and lower-middle-class existence because it cannot be made heroic or comedic.
And then in the second passage he goes further — he insists on what I'd call the aesthetics of frustration.
He tells Reardon: 'When the man and woman are to meet for a great scene of passion, let it all be frustrated by one or other of them having a bad cold in the head.'
This is not whimsy — it is a structural argument that drama itself is a class privilege.
When your life is constrained by paltry circumstance, the narrative arc of romantic passion is not available to you.
I find Daniel's reading compelling on the aesthetic plane, though I'd resist the instinct to flatten it into ideology.
What Gissing seems to me to be defending is something more intimate — a kind of character that is simply unsuited to the world as constituted.
There is a passage in Chapter 31 where the narrator intervenes directly — and it is one of the most explicitly argued passages in the book.
He writes: 'These two were richly endowed with the kindly and the imaginative virtues; if fate threw them amid incongruous circumstances, is their endowment of less value?'
'You scorn their passivity; but it was their nature and their merit to be passive.'
That is the narrator stepping in front of the reader and making a moral argument — not a political one.
The question is not what the system does to these men — it is whether we have the imaginative generosity to value what they are.
What strikes me as a reader — a performer of this text — is how Gissing uses Reardon himself to embody the contradiction Edmund is describing.
Early in the novel, the narrator gives us this extraordinarily candid account of Reardon's temperament.
'He was the kind of man who cannot struggle against adverse conditions, but whom prosperity warms to the exercise of his powers.'
That sentence is doing something formally daring — the narrator is telling us, quite early on, exactly how this story must end.
There is no suspense about whether Reardon will overcome adversity — the novel has already told you he cannot.
The only question is what shape the falling will take, and how beautiful Gissing can make the observation of it.
Oliver puts his finger on something crucial about the novel's form — it does not build toward revelation, it documents inevitability.
And Reardon himself arrives at a formulation of this that is almost unbearable to read.
He says: 'To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort of anticipation of death.'
'The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead.'
'And what remains of me is resigned to that. I have an odd fancy that it will make death itself easier; it is as if only half of me had now to die.'
He has understood that his social death — his erasure from the literary market — precedes and in some sense produces his physical death.
The market does not merely fail Reardon — it kills him, in instalments, while he watches.
I would not quarrel with that reading, though I'd say Reardon's tragedy is also moral — he chooses, at crucial moments, wrongly.
But what Gissing achieves formally — and this is what the form-and-decay question is really about — is a narrative that refuses the consolations of plot.
No reversal, no redemption, no last chapter recovery.
The novel practices what Biffen preaches — even unto its own shape.
Form and content in absolute alignment — perhaps the most demanding thing a novelist can attempt.
And it leaves us with a final question that I think we have to face: what does it cost, individually and culturally, to be the kind of artist Gissing describes?
That's where we're heading next — the price of ambition in an industrial literary culture.

segments.title: Closing: The Cost of Ambition in Industrial Culture

utterances.text: We've been exploring how Gissing shapes his novel's form to mirror its world of decay and pressure.
Now, in this final stretch, I want to ask what that world actually costs — the human price of literary ambition in an industrial culture.
The cost is written most clearly in Marian Yule — and Gissing knows it.
She is the most acute diagnostician in the whole novel, and she delivers her verdict in a single outburst.
She's speaking to her father, watching how the literary world has warped his capacity for honest judgment.
"I wish I could have done for ever with the hateful profession that so poisons men's minds."
That word — poisons — is doing enormous work.
It's not that the literary market is disappointing or demoralising — it is actively toxic, corrupting judgment at the root.
And it's a woman who sees it most clearly — the person the system has least rewarded and most used.
I don't resist that reading — Marian's suffering is genuine and Gissing honours it fully.
But what strikes me is that her accusation is also a portrait of Alfred Yule's moral failure — his vanity, his pettiness, his surrender to envy.
The literary market does not compel a man to become petty and dishonest.
It provides the occasion; character provides the response.
Gissing, I would argue, is far too good a novelist to simply indict an institution.
He is always asking: what does this circumstance reveal about this particular soul?
Both of you are right, and that is what makes Marian so unforgettable — she contains both verdicts at once.
And then there's that extraordinary passage in chapter thirty, where Gissing renders her state through the London fog.
As a performer, I find it almost unbearable to read aloud, and I mean that as the highest praise.
"The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be smelt and tasted."
"Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul."
The bottomless pit — Gissing reaches straight into Dante for that image.
And notice it appears in this novel about literary journalism, not in some grand historical epic.
That is Gissing's audacity — he insists that this world deserves that scale of moral seriousness.
And then set that against Jasper Milvain — who breathes the same air and flourishes.
Because Jasper doesn't suffer — he simply strips away every pretence and says out loud what the market actually demands.
He puts it with disarming directness — and this is what makes him so chilling as a character.
"Nearly all men who have their way to make think as I do, but most feel obliged to adopt a false tone, to talk about literary conscientiousness, and so on."
"I simply say what I think, with no pretences. I should like to be conscientious, but it's a luxury I can't afford."
A luxury he can't afford.
Conscience has been fully absorbed into the language of market economics.
What Marian names as poison, Jasper has simply learned to drink without flinching.
And that is precisely why Jasper is not a villain in any simple sense — Gissing doesn't allow us that comfort.
He is too self-aware, too candid, too intelligent.
Johnson observed that a man who is tired of London is tired of life.
One might adapt that: a reader who is comfortable with Jasper Milvain has perhaps made his peace with too much.
The novel will not let us simply admire his efficiency and move on.
Gissing insists on placing Marian's anguish — that reek of the bottomless pit — directly beside Jasper's cheerful careerism.
The juxtaposition is the moral argument.
That juxtaposition works in performance too — the tonal gap between those two worlds is enormous and Gissing maintains it without ever tipping into melodrama.
Jasper is almost breezy — you can hear it in how his sentences move, quick and confident.
And then you come to Marian lying in that fog — her face colourless as the pillow — and the prose goes almost still.
That is Gissing controlling his instrument with complete mastery.
He's not arguing at you — he's making you feel the difference in your body.
What a place to end — Gissing making us feel the argument rather than merely stating it.
We have moved today through the novel's ambitions and its ruins: the machinery of literary London, the characters broken and bent by it, the prose that registers every fracture.
My deepest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, whose ear for the novel's voice and comic genius has been a constant pleasure.
To Sir Edmund Leigh, who has kept us honest about character, conscience, and the limits of any single reading.
And to Daniel Rosen, whose insistence on the system behind every suffering has sharpened everything we've seen.
New Grub Street is a novel that knows exactly what it costs to want things in a world that prices everything.
We hope it's sent you back to the book — or to it for the first time.
Thank you for listening to New Grub Street Unpacked.

c27:p121.text:
They repaired to the haunt in question. A flight of stairs brought them to
      a small room in which were exposed the daily newspapers; another ascent,
      and they were in a room devoted to magazines, chess, and refreshments; yet
      another, and they reached the department of weekly publications; lastly,
      at the top of the house, they found a lavatory, and a chamber for the use
      of those who desired to write. The walls of this last retreat were of blue
      plaster and sloped inwards from the floor; along them stood school desks
      with benches, and in one place was suspended a ragged and dirty card
      announcing that paper and envelopes could be purchased downstairs. An
      enormous basket full of waste-paper, and a small stove, occupied two
      corners; ink blotches, satirical designs, and much scribbling in pen and
      pencil served for mural adornment. From the adjacent lavatory came sounds
      of splashing and spluttering, and the busy street far below sent up its
      confused noises.
c27:p121.summary: Gissing provides a detailed topography of the penny reading-room: successive floors with newspapers, magazines, chess, and finally a writing-room with sloped blue walls, school desks, a trash basket, a small stove, and walls decorated with scribbling and ink blotches.
c27:p121.best_quote: The walls of this last retreat were of blue plaster and sloped inwards from the floor; along them stood school desks with benches, and in one place was suspended a ragged and dirty card announcing that paper and envelopes could be purchased downstairs.

c27:p105.text:
‘With what magnificent scorn they would turn from us and our squalid
      feast! They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school
      men, University men, club men, society men. An income of less than three
      or four hundred a year is inconceivable to them; that seems the minimum
      for an educated man’s support. It would be small-minded to think of them
      with rancour, but, by Apollo! I know that we should change places with
      them if the work we have done were justly weighed against theirs.’
c27:p105.summary: Reardon condemns the successful novelists as public-school men incapable of understanding poverty; he insists their literary work is inferior to his own but serves the market demand, and asserts that if true merit were weighed, he and Biffen would triumph.
c27:p105.best_quote: They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school men, University men, club men, society men.

c15:p0.text:
The past twelve months had added several years to Edwin Reardon’s seeming
      age; at thirty-three he would generally have been taken for forty. His
      bearing, his personal habits, were no longer those of a young man; he
      walked with a stoop and pressed noticeably on the stick he carried; it was
      rare for him to show the countenance which tells of present cheerfulness
      or glad onward-looking; there was no spring in his step; his voice had
      fallen to a lower key, and often he spoke with that hesitation in choice
      of words which may be noticed in persons whom defeat has made
      self-distrustful. Ceaseless perplexity and dread gave a wandering,
      sometimes a wild, expression to his eyes.
c15:p0.summary: Reardon has aged dramatically in the past year, his body and bearing showing the ravages of mental strain and deprivation; he moves with difficulty, sleeps poorly, and his eyes show wild distress.
c15:p0.best_quote: at thirty-three he would generally have been taken for forty

c4:p84.text:
‘And yet,’ he continued, ‘of course it isn’t only for the sake of
      reputation that one tries to do uncommon work. There’s the shrinking from
      conscious insincerity of workmanship—which most of the writers
      nowadays seem never to feel. “It’s good enough for the market”; that
      satisfies them. And perhaps they are justified.
c4:p84.summary: Edwin continues his meditation: he cannot rule his life by absolute ideals; everything is relative. Yet he cannot help but try to make his work good, even knowing it can't be first-rate—a contradiction he acknowledges.
c4:p84.best_quote: There's the shrinking from conscious insincerity of workmanship—which most of the writers nowadays seem never to feel.

c15:p93.text:
‘Darling, they do struggle. But it’s as if an ever-increasing weight were
      round their necks; it drags them lower and lower. The world has no pity on
      a man who can’t do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be
      a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn’t take pity on you you will
      starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate. I have no
      right to complain of my own ill-fortune; it’s my own fault (in a sense)
      that I can’t continue as well as I began; if I could write books as good
      as the early ones I should earn money. For all that, it’s hard that I must
      be kicked aside as worthless just because I don’t know a trade.’
c15:p93.summary: Reardon argues that despite the efforts of struggling men with families, an ever-increasing burden drags them down; society is indifferent to human worth and offers no mercy to those without marketable skills; he accepts some personal responsibility but indicts the system as cruel and blind.
c15:p93.best_quote: The world has no pity on a man who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn't take pity on you you will starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate.

c6:p93.text:
‘That half-year abroad, and the extraordinary shock of happiness which
      followed at once upon it, have disturbed the balance of my nature. It was
      adjusted to circumstances of hardship, privation, struggle. A temperament
      like mine can’t pass through such a violent change of conditions without
      being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I
      left England. The stage I had then reached was the result of a slow and
      elaborate building up; I could look back and see the processes by which I
      had grown from the boy who was a mere bookworm to the man who had all but
      succeeded as a novelist. It was a perfectly natural, sober development.
      But in the last two years and a half I can distinguish no order. In living
      through it, I have imagined from time to time that my powers were coming
      to their ripest; but that was mere delusion. Intellectually, I have fallen
      back. The probability is that this wouldn’t matter, if only I could live
      on in peace of mind; I should recover my equilibrium, and perhaps once
      more understand myself. But the due course of things is troubled by my
      poverty.’
c6:p93.summary: Reardon analyzes how his sojourn abroad and the subsequent shock of happiness with Amy disrupted his previously balanced development, leading to intellectual decline and mental paralysis aggravated by financial desperation; he contrasts his formerly natural development with his current disordered state.
c6:p93.best_quote: A temperament like mine can't pass through such a violent change of conditions without being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I left England... I have imagined from time to time that my powers were coming to their ripest; but that was mere delusion. Intellectually, I have fallen back... But the due course of things is troubled by my poverty.

c12:p1.text:
Between him and her there was no longer perfect confidence. Her silence
      meant reproach, and—whatever might have been the case before—there
      was no doubt that she now discussed him with her mother, possibly with
      other people. It was not likely that she concealed his own opinion of the
      book he had just finished; all their acquaintances would be prepared to
      greet its publication with private scoffing or with mournful shaking of
      the head. His feeling towards Amy entered upon a new phase. The stability
      of his love was a source of pain; condemning himself, he felt at the same
      time that he was wronged. A coldness which was far from representing the
      truth began to affect his manner and speech, and Amy did not seem to
      notice it, at all events she made no kind of protest. They no longer
      talked of the old subjects, but of those mean concerns of material life
      which formerly they had agreed to dismiss as quickly as possible. Their
      relations to each other—not long ago an inexhaustible topic—would
      not bear spoken comment; both were too conscious of the danger-signal when
      they looked that way.
c12:p1.summary: The novel traces how Amy's silence and discussions with her mother have broken Reardon's confidence in their marriage; they have shifted from discussing intimate matters to mere practical concerns of survival.
c12:p1.best_quote: Their relations to each other—not long ago an inexhaustible topic—would not bear spoken comment; both were too conscious of the danger-signal when they looked that way.

c17:p87.text:
Could Amy’s voice sound like that? Great Heaven! With just such accent he
      had heard a wrangling woman retort upon her husband at the street corner.
      Is there then no essential difference between a woman of this world and
      one of that? Does the same nature lie beneath such unlike surfaces?
c17:p87.summary: Reardon realizes Amy's voice and manner now resemble a lower-class quarreling woman, and he wonders if character is determined entirely by circumstance.
c17:p87.best_quote: With just such accent he had heard a wrangling woman retort upon her husband at the street corner. Is there then no essential difference between a woman of this world and one of that?

c16:p125.text:
‘It seems to me, Amy, that your one desire is to get away from me, on
      whatever terms.’
c16:p125.summary: Reardon accuses Amy of wanting nothing more than to escape him and their marriage.
c16:p125.best_quote: It seems to me, Amy, that your one desire is to get away from me, on whatever terms.

c1:p43.text:
‘To be sure! To be sure!’ exclaimed their brother. ‘You have no faith. But
      just understand the difference between a man like Reardon and a man like
      me. He is the old type of unpractical artist; I am the literary man of
      1882. He won’t make concessions, or rather, he can’t make them; he can’t
      supply the market. I—well, you may say that at present I do nothing;
      but that’s a great mistake, I am learning my business. Literature nowadays
      is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic
      force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman. He thinks
      first and foremost of the markets; when one kind of goods begins to go off
      slackly, he is ready with something new and appetising. He knows perfectly
      all the possible sources of income. Whatever he has to sell he’ll get
      payment for it from all sorts of various quarters; none of your
      unpractical selling for a lump sum to a middleman who will make six
      distinct profits. Now, look you: if I had been in Reardon’s place, I’d
      have made four hundred at least out of “The Optimist”; I should have gone
      shrewdly to work with magazines and newspapers and foreign publishers, and—all
      sorts of people. Reardon can’t do that kind of thing, he’s behind his age;
      he sells a manuscript as if he lived in Sam Johnson’s Grub Street. But our
      Grub Street of to-day is quite a different place: it is supplied with
      telegraphic communication, it knows what literary fare is in demand in
      every part of the world, its inhabitants are men of business, however
      seedy.’
c1:p43.summary: Jasper articulates his philosophy: literature is a business, not an art; successful writers are those who understand the market and supply it strategically. He contrasts Reardon's 'old' unpractical approach with his own 'new' commercial method, emphasizing that writers must exploit all sources of income, manipulate magazines and newspapers, and treat their work as marketable goods rather than selling manuscripts for a lump sum like Samuel Johnson's era.
c1:p43.best_quote: Literature nowadays is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman.

c14:p63.text:
‘Not unfortunate at all. I had to crack him up; otherwise I couldn’t have
      done the job so quickly. It’s the easiest thing in the world to write
      laudation; only an inexperienced grumbler would declare it was easier to
      find fault. The book was Billington’s “Vagaries”; pompous idiocy, of
      course, but he lives in a big house and gives dinners. Well, from 10.30 to
      11, I smoked a cigar and reflected, feeling that the day wasn’t badly
      begun. At eleven I was ready to write my Saturday causerie for the Will o’
      the Wisp; it took me till close upon one o’clock, which was rather too
      long. I can’t afford more than an hour and a half for that job. At one, I
      rushed out to a dirty little eating-house in Hampstead Road. Was back
      again by a quarter to two, having in the meantime sketched a paper for The
      West End. Pipe in mouth, I sat down to leisurely artistic work; by five,
      half the paper was done; the other half remains for to-morrow. From five
      to half-past I read four newspapers and two magazines, and from half-past
      to a quarter to six I jotted down several ideas that had come to me whilst
      reading. At six I was again in the dirty eating-house, satisfying a
      ferocious hunger. Home once more at 6.45, and for two hours wrote steadily
      at a long affair I have in hand for The Current. Then I came here,
      thinking hard all the way. What say you to this? Have I earned a night’s
      repose?’
c14:p63.summary: Jasper explains he wrote glowing praise of Billington's 'Vagaries' because the author is wealthy and socially connected, making positive reviews easy and lucrative.
c14:p63.best_quote: It's the easiest thing in the world to write laudation; only an inexperienced grumbler would declare it was easier to find fault.

c6:p63.text:
‘’Tis my vocation, Hal! You might think I hadn’t experience enough, to
      begin with. But my intuition is so strong that I can make a little
      experience go an immense way. Most people would imagine I had been wasting
      my time these last few years, just sauntering about, reading nothing but
      periodicals, making acquaintance with loafers of every description. The
      truth is, I have been collecting ideas, and ideas that are convertible
      into coin of the realm, my boy; I have the special faculty of an extempore
      writer. Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value; I
      shall always despise the people I write for. But my path will be that of
      success. I have always said it, and now I’m sure of it.’
c6:p63.summary: Jasper defends his unconventional path to success, claiming that despite appearing to waste time, he has been collecting convertible ideas and has a special faculty for extempore writing. He frankly admits he will never produce solid literature and will despise his audience, but insists success is assured.
c6:p63.best_quote: My intuition is so strong that I can make a little experience go an immense way... I have the special faculty of an extempore writer. Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value; I shall always despise the people I write for. But my path will be that of success.

c4:p55.text:
‘How very silly it is to talk like this!’ came in Amy’s voice, clearly
      critical. ‘Art must be practised as a trade, at all events in our time.
      This is the age of trade. Of course if one refuses to be of one’s time,
      and yet hasn’t the means to live independently, what can result but
      breakdown and wretchedness? The fact of the matter is, you could do fairly
      good work, and work which would sell, if only you would bring yourself to
      look at things in a more practical way. It’s what Mr Milvain is always
      saying, you know.’
c4:p55.summary: Amy argues that art must be practiced as commerce in the modern age; refusing to adapt while lacking independent means leads only to failure. She cites Jasper Milvain as an example of practical success.
c4:p55.best_quote: Art must be practised as a trade, at all events in our time. This is the age of trade. Of course if one refuses to be of one's time, and yet hasn't the means to live independently, what can result but breakdown and wretchedness?

c8:p180.text:
‘I like to hear people say that, but it’ll mean savage work. When we were
      all at Finden last year, I told the girls that it would be another twelve
      months before I could support myself. Now I am forced to do it. And I
      don’t like work; my nature is lazy. I shall never write for writing’s
      sake, only to make money. All my plans and efforts will have money in view—all.
      I shan’t allow anything to come in the way of my material advancement.’
c8:p180.summary: Jasper bluntly states he will not write for its own sake, that all his efforts serve material advancement, and that he lacks the natural inclination toward work.
c8:p180.best_quote: I shan't allow anything to come in the way of my material advancement.

c8:p11.text:
She went up to her room, and wept over the wretchedness of all their
      lives. Her loneliness had seemed harder to bear than ever since that last
      holiday. For a moment, in the lanes about Finden, there had come to her a
      vision of joy such as fate owed her youth; but it had faded, and she could
      no longer hope for its return. She was not a woman, but a mere machine for
      reading and writing. Did her father never think of this? He was not the
      only one to suffer from the circumstances in which poverty had involved
      him.
c8:p11.summary: In her room, Marian weeps over the misery of her family's circumstances, recalling her brief moment of happiness at Finden and mourning her lost opportunity for love.
c8:p11.best_quote: She was not a woman, but a mere machine for reading and writing.

c14:p147.text:
Marian often went thus far in her speculation. Her candour was allied with
      clear insight into the possibilities of falsehood; she was not readily the
      victim of illusion; thinking much, and speaking little, she had not come
      to her twenty-third year without perceiving what a distance lay between a
      girl’s dream of life as it might be and life as it is. Had she invariably
      disclosed her thoughts, she would have earned the repute of a very
      sceptical and slightly cynical person.
c14:p147.summary: Marian's character is defined by candid perception of human hypocrisy and the gap between ideals and reality; she would be regarded as cynical if she spoke her thoughts aloud.
c14:p147.best_quote: Her candour was allied with clear insight into the possibilities of falsehood; she was not readily the victim of illusion; thinking much, and speaking little, she had not come to her twenty-third year without perceiving what a distance lay between a girl's dream of life as it might be and life as it is.

c8:p15.text:
One day at the end of the month she sat with books open before her, but by
      no effort could fix her attention upon them. It was gloomy, and one could
      scarcely see to read; a taste of fog grew perceptible in the warm,
      headachy air. Such profound discouragement possessed her that she could
      not even maintain the pretence of study; heedless whether anyone observed
      her, she let her hands fall and her head droop. She kept asking herself
      what was the use and purpose of such a life as she was condemned to lead.
      When already there was more good literature in the world than any mortal
      could cope with in his lifetime, here was she exhausting herself in the
      manufacture of printed stuff which no one even pretended to be more than a
      commodity for the day’s market. What unspeakable folly! To write—was
      not that the joy and the privilege of one who had an urgent message for
      the world?
c8:p15.summary: In the Museum on a gloomy day, Marian's concentration collapses as she questions the purpose of manufacturing literature for market consumption when the world already contains more books than anyone can read.
c8:p15.best_quote: What unspeakable folly! To write—was not that the joy and the privilege of one who had an urgent message for the world?

c14:p157.text:
The unhoped was all but granted her. She could labour on in the valley of
      the shadow of books, for a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment
      strike into its musty gloom.
c14:p157.summary: Marian concludes her reflections with hope: she can endure her dreary library work because love promises to illuminate her darkness.
c14:p157.best_quote: She could labour on in the valley of the shadow of books, for a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment strike into its musty gloom.

c1:p98.text:
‘Inferior? Oh, if you can be a George Eliot, begin at the earliest
      opportunity. I merely suggested what seemed practicable.
      But I don’t think you have genius, Maud. People have got that ancient
      prejudice so firmly rooted in their heads—that one mustn’t write
      save at the dictation of the Holy Spirit. I tell you, writing is a
      business. Get together half-a-dozen fair specimens of the Sunday-school
      prize; study them; discover the essential points of such composition; hit
      upon new attractions; then go to work methodically, so many pages a day.
      There’s no question of the divine afflatus; that belongs to another sphere
      of life. We talk of literature as a trade, not of Homer, Dante, and
      Shakespeare. If I could only get that into poor Reardon’s head. He thinks
      me a gross beast, often enough. What the devil—I mean what on earth
      is there in typography to make everything it deals with sacred? I don’t
      advocate the propagation of vicious literature; I speak only of good,
      coarse, marketable stuff for the world’s vulgar. You just give it a
      thought, Maud; talk it over with Dora.’
c1:p98.summary: Jasper insists that writing is a business, not an art requiring divine afflatus; he advocates studying successful prize-books, identifying their formulaic elements, then producing similar work methodically. He defends supplying the 'mob' with marketable goods, dismisses artistic pretension, and contrasts moral high-mindedness with practical success. He mentions Reardon's disapproval and reveals his philosophy: write for the upper-middle-class intelligentsia who desire clever work but cannot distinguish 'stones and paste.' He notes his own recent success in The West End.
c1:p98.best_quote: Writing is a business. Get together half-a-dozen fair specimens of the Sunday-school prize; study them; discover the essential points of such composition; hit upon new attractions; then go to work methodically, so many pages a day.

c1:p100.text:
‘I maintain that we people of brains are justified in supplying the mob
      with the food it likes. We are not geniuses, and if we sit down in a
      spirit of long-eared gravity we shall produce only commonplace stuff. Let
      us use our wits to earn money, and make the best we can of our lives. If
      only I had the skill, I would produce novels out-trashing the trashiest
      that ever sold fifty thousand copies. But it needs skill, mind you: and to
      deny it is a gross error of the literary pedants. To please the vulgar you
      must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity. For my own
      part, I shan’t be able to address the bulkiest multitude; my talent
      doesn’t lend itself to that form. I shall write for the upper middle-class
      of intellect, the people who like to feel that what they are reading has
      some special cleverness, but who can’t distinguish between stones and
      paste. That’s why I’m so slow in warming to the work. Every month I feel
      surer of myself, however.
c1:p100.summary: Jasper argues that people of talent should supply the mob's preferred fare, not sit in solemn gravity producing commonplace work. He emphasises that skill is required to create commercially successful trash. He will not address the mass market; instead he targets the upper-middle-class intelligentsia who desire clever work. He notes his monthly growing confidence and cites his recent West End piece as proof of his ability to hit the mark.
c1:p100.best_quote: To please the vulgar you must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity.

c13:p2.text:
The May number of The Current, in its article headed ‘Books of the Month,’
      devoted about half a page to ‘English Prose in the Nineteenth Century.’
      This notice was a consummate example of the flippant style of attack.
      Flippancy, the most hopeless form of intellectual vice, was a
      characterising note of Mr Fadge’s periodical; his monthly comments on
      publications were already looked for with eagerness by that growing class
      of readers who care for nothing but what can be made matter of ridicule.
      The hostility of other reviewers was awkward and ineffectual compared with
      this venomous banter, which entertained by showing that in the book under
      notice there was neither entertainment nor any other kind of interest. To
      assail an author without increasing the number of his readers is the
      perfection of journalistic skill, and The Current, had it stood alone,
      would fully have achieved this end. As it was, silence might have been
      better tactics. But Mr Fadge knew that his enemy would smart under the
      poisoned pin-points, and that was something gained.
c13:p2.summary: The Current's review of Yule's book exemplifies the flippancy and venomous banter characteristic of Fadge's editorial approach, designed to entertain readers who seek only ridicule rather than genuine literary criticism.
c13:p2.best_quote: To assail an author without increasing the number of his readers is the perfection of journalistic skill

c27:p122.text:
Two persons only sat at the desks. One was a hunger-bitten, out-of-work
      clerk, evidently engaged in replying to advertisements; in front of him
      lay two or three finished letters, and on the ground at his feet were
      several crumpled sheets of note-paper, representing abortive essays in
      composition. The other man, also occupied with the pen, looked about forty
      years old, and was clad in a very rusty suit of tweeds; on the bench
      beside him lay a grey overcoat and a silk hat which had for some time been
      moulting. His face declared the habit to which he was a victim, but it had
      nothing repulsive in its lineaments and expression; on the contrary, it
      was pleasing, amiable, and rather quaint. At this moment no one would have
      doubted his sobriety. With coat-sleeve turned back, so as to give free
      play to his right hand and wrist, revealing meanwhile a flannel shirt of
      singular colour, and with his collar unbuttoned (he wore no tie) to leave
      his throat at ease as he bent myopically over the paper, he was writing at
      express speed, evidently in the full rush of the ardour of composition.
      The veins of his forehead were dilated, and his chin pushed forward in a
      way that made one think of a racing horse.
c27:p122.summary: Gissing describes Sykes at work at his desk: a shabby, alcoholic figure in rusty tweeds with grey overcoat and moulting silk hat, yet fully absorbed in rapid composition, veins dilated and chin thrust forward like a racing horse.
c27:p122.best_quote: With coat-sleeve turned back, so as to give free play to his right hand and wrist, revealing meanwhile a flannel shirt of singular colour, and with his collar unbuttoned (he wore no tie) to leave his throat at ease as he bent myopically over the paper, he was writing at express speed, evidently in the full rush of the ardour of composition.

c10:p119.text:
‘I have thought of a new way of putting it. What I really aim at is an
      absolute realism in the sphere of the ignobly decent. The field, as I
      understand it, is a new one; I don’t know any writer who has treated
      ordinary vulgar life with fidelity and seriousness. Zola writes deliberate
      tragedies; his vilest figures become heroic from the place they fill in a
      strongly imagined drama. I want to deal with the essentially unheroic,
      with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the
      mercy of paltry circumstance. Dickens understood the possibility of such
      work, but his tendency to melodrama on the one hand, and his humour on the
      other, prevented him from thinking of it. An instance, now. As I came
      along by Regent’s Park half an hour ago a man and a girl were walking
      close in front of me, love-making; I passed them slowly and heard a good
      deal of their talk—it was part of the situation that they should pay
      no heed to a stranger’s proximity. Now, such a love-scene as that has
      absolutely never been written down; it was entirely decent, yet vulgar to
      the nth power. Dickens would have made it ludicrous—a gross
      injustice. Other men who deal with low-class life would perhaps have
      preferred idealising it—an absurdity. For my own part, I am going to
      reproduce it verbatim, without one single impertinent suggestion of any
      point of view save that of honest reporting. The result will be something
      unutterably tedious. Precisely. That is the stamp of the ignobly decent
      life. If it were anything but tedious it would be untrue. I speak, of
      course, of its effect upon the ordinary reader.’
c10:p119.summary: Biffen expounds his theory of absolute realism applied to ordinary, vulgar life—rejecting both Zola's melodrama and Dickens's humor, insisting instead on verbatim reproduction of the tedious, unheroic reality of common people.
c10:p119.best_quote: I want to deal with the essentially unheroic, with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the mercy of paltry circumstance

c10:p137.text:
‘It is worked out. We must have a rest from it. You, now—the best
      things you have done are altogether in conflict with novelistic
      conventionalities. It was because that blackguard review of “On Neutral
      Ground” clumsily hinted this that I first thought of you with interest.
      No, no; let us copy life. When the man and woman are to meet for a great
      scene of passion, let it all be frustrated by one or other of them having
      a bad cold in the head, and so on. Let the pretty girl get a disfiguring
      pimple on her nose just before the ball at which she is going to shine.
      Show the numberless repulsive features of common decent life. Seriously,
      coldly; not a hint of facetiousness, or the thing becomes different.’
c10:p137.summary: Biffen argues that realist fiction should reject dramatic convention in favor of mundane reality: love scenes interrupted by illness, beauty spoiled by pimples.
c10:p137.best_quote: When the man and woman are to meet for a great scene of passion, let it all be frustrated by one or other of them having a bad cold in the head

c31:p1.text:
But try to imagine a personality wholly unfitted for the rough and tumble
      of the world’s labour-market. From the familiar point of view these men
      were worthless; view them in possible relation to a humane order of
      Society, and they are admirable citizens. Nothing is easier than to
      condemn a type of character which is unequal to the coarse demands of life
      as it suits the average man. These two were richly endowed with the kindly
      and the imaginative virtues; if fate threw them amid incongruous
      circumstances, is their endowment of less value? You scorn their
      passivity; but it was their nature and their merit to be passive.
c31:p1.summary: The narrator defends Reardon and Biffen as admirable in a humane society, arguing their passivity is a merit rather than a failing.
c31:p1.best_quote: These two were richly endowed with the kindly and the imaginative virtues; if fate threw them amid incongruous circumstances, is their endowment of less value?

c5:p34.text:
He was the kind of man who cannot struggle against adverse conditions, but
      whom prosperity warms to the exercise of his powers. Anything like the
      cares of responsibility would sooner or later harass him into
      unproductiveness. That he should produce much was in any case out of the
      question; possibly a book every two or three years might not prove too
      great a strain upon his delicate mental organism, but for him to attempt
      more than that would certainly be fatal to the peculiar merit of his work.
      Of this he was dimly conscious, and, on receiving his legacy, he put aside
      for nearly twelve months the new novel he had begun. To give his mind a
      rest he wrote several essays, much maturer than those which had formerly
      failed to find acceptance, and two of these appeared in magazines.
c5:p34.summary: Reardon is psychologically dependent on ease and cannot produce much without damaging his artistic integrity; he rests and writes essays before resuming novel-writing.
c5:p34.best_quote: He was the kind of man who cannot struggle against adverse conditions, but whom prosperity warms to the exercise of his powers.

c31:p89.text:
‘To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort
      of anticipation of death. The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes
      spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead. And what
      remains of me is resigned to that. I have an odd fancy that it will make
      death itself easier; it is as if only half of me had now to die.’
c31:p89.summary: Reardon philosophizes that outliving his reputation is a kind of death; he feels the person he was is already dead.
c31:p89.best_quote: To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort of anticipation of death. The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead. And what remains of me is resigned to that. I have an odd fancy that it will make death itself easier; it is as if only half of me had now to die.

c21:p105.text:
‘Literary quarrels have made you incapable of judging honestly in things
      such as this. I wish I could have done for ever with the hateful
      profession that so poisons men’s minds.’
c21:p105.summary: Marian attacks the literary profession, saying that literary quarrels have poisoned her father's ability to judge honestly and wishing she could be forever done with it.
c21:p105.best_quote: I wish I could have done for ever with the hateful profession that so poisons men's minds

c30:p150.text:
The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be
      smelt and tasted. Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in
      the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek
      of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul. Her face colourless as the
      pillow, Marian lay neither sleeping nor awake, in blank extremity of woe;
      tears now and then ran down her cheeks, and at times her body was shaken
      with a throe such as might result from anguish of the torture chamber.
c30:p150.summary: The narrator evokes the oppressive London fog as a physical manifestation of Marian's emotional anguish; it is almost Dantean in its suggestion of hellish suffering.
c30:p150.best_quote: The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be smelt and tasted. Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul

c24:p54.text:
‘That’s precisely the truth. Nearly all men who have their way to make
      think as I do, but most feel obliged to adopt a false tone, to talk about
      literary conscientiousness, and so on. I simply say what I think, with no
      pretences. I should like to be conscientious, but it’s a luxury I can’t
      afford. I’ve told you all this often enough, you know.’
c24:p54.summary: Jasper argues that most aspiring writers share his pragmatic views but hide them; he alone speaks honestly about the necessity of worldly ambition.
c24:p54.best_quote: Nearly all men who have their way to make think as I do, but most feel obliged to adopt a false tone, to talk about literary conscientiousness, and so on. I simply say what I think, with no pretences. I should like to be conscientious, but it's a luxury I can't afford.
